content_summary: Bypassing Android Decoder Macroblock Limits with Dual-Strip NVENC Tiling
content_full_text:
The tablet screen is native 2560x1600, but its hardware video decoder flatly refuses any frame that size.

While building usb-display (turning an Android tablet into a native Windows extended monitor over USB), we hit a hard silicon boundary: the MediaTek video decoder is hard-capped at 14,400 macroblocks per frame. A 2560x1600 frame requires 16,000. All 14 decoders exposed by the device rejected it at configure() time.

Yet the GPU drives the 2560x1600 panel effortlessly. That gap made the workaround possible:

1. Windows host captures the virtual display via Desktop Duplication API.
2. Frame is split into two 2560x800 horizontal strips (8,000 macroblocks each — safely below the 14,400 ceiling).
3. Both strips are encoded concurrently using NVIDIA NVENC hardware encoding.
4. Streamed over TCP through an adb reverse tunnel across the USB cable.
5. Android app decodes each strip in its own MediaCodec instance directly onto adjacent SurfaceViews.

Why two strips instead of four? We benchmarked instance scaling:
- 1 instance @ 2560x800: 49.4 fps (395k macroblocks/s)
- 2 instances @ 2560x800: 43.2 fps (691k macroblocks/s)
- 3 instances @ 2560x800: 28.9 fps (per-instance collapse)
- 4 instances @ 2560x800: 23.0 fps

Because the display runs at the slowest strip's rate, two strips is the mathematical optimum.

Measured outcome: 45.3 fps sustained native playback over 146 seconds of 4K video with zero dropped frames. Bitrate averaged 20.0 Mbit/s — roughly 7% of what USB 2.0 carries.

When streaming low-latency video to mobile devices, the cable bandwidth is rarely the bottleneck. The fixed-function decoder silicon is.
